Linear Momentum: Linear momentum is the product of an object mass and its velocity, p = mv. It is a vector that points in the direction of the velocity, and its SI unit is the kilogram meter per second. A heavier or faster object has more momentum. Doubling the speed doubles the momentum but quadruples the kinetic energy, which is related by KE = p^2 / (2m). Momentum is the quantity that Newton second law really changes, since the net force equals the rate of change of momentum, F = delta p / delta t.
Impulse and the Impulse-Momentum Theorem: Impulse is the product of the average force and the time it acts, J = F delta t, measured in newton seconds, which equal kg m/s. The impulse-momentum theorem states that impulse equals the change in momentum, F delta t = m vf - m vi. For a given momentum change, a longer contact time means a smaller average force, which is why airbags, helmets and padding protect people. A rebound gives a larger change than a simple stop, because the velocity reverses direction.
Conservation of Momentum: The law of conservation of momentum says that the total momentum of a system stays constant when no net external force acts on it. In any interaction inside an isolated system, the momentum gained by one object equals the momentum lost by another. To solve problems, choose a positive direction, write the total momentum before and after, and set them equal. This explains recoil of a gun, the push-off of skaters, explosions that start at rest, and rockets, where the total momentum stays zero.
Elastic and Inelastic Collisions: In every collision of an isolated system, total momentum is conserved. Kinetic energy distinguishes the types. In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is also conserved and the objects bounce apart. In an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound or deformation. In a perfectly inelastic collision the objects stick and move together with the common velocity v = (m1 v1 + m2 v2) / (m1 + m2), which loses the most kinetic energy. Equal masses in a head-on elastic collision exchange velocities.
Circular Motion and Gravitation: An object in uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity, so it accelerates toward the center with centripetal acceleration a = v^2 / r and needs a net inward centripetal force F = m v^2 / r. The speed is v = 2 pi r / T. Newton law of universal gravitation states that every two masses attract with a force F = G m1 m2 / r^2, where G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2. Gravity supplies the centripetal force for planets and satellites, giving orbital speed v = sqrt(G M / r).
